opus-5.5.text:
I think the core reason is that embodied intelligence works very differently from the kind of work a large company usually does. At a big company, much of the work is about software, services, and platforms. You iterate quickly online, you have huge numbers of users, and the feedback loop is fast. Embodied intelligence touches the physical world. You deal with hardware, supply chains, data collection in real environments, safety, and deployment in actual scenarios. The rhythm, the talent, and even how you measure progress are all different.

If you keep this inside a big organization as one more project, it's easy for it to be judged by the same standards as everything else, like short-term metrics or how it fits existing businesses. Embodied intelligence needs patience. A lot of the foundational problems, like how to get enough high-quality data, how to make a model generalize across tasks and bodies, and how to close the loop between perception, decision, and action, won't be solved in one or two quarters.

A separate entity gives you focus. The team can think from first principles about what this field needs and organize around that. It can bring in people from robotics, mechanical engineering, and control as well as AI, and build a culture that fits a startup working on hard problems. It also makes partnerships with hardware makers, research institutions, and industry partners more natural, because you're seen as a dedicated player in the field rather than a side effort of a bigger company.

At the same time, you're not starting from zero. You can still draw on the parent company's strengths in large models, compute, engineering infrastructure, and understanding of real-world scenarios. So I see it as getting the best of both: the focus and agility of a startup, with the resources and long-term backing of a large organization. For something as early and as hard as embodied intelligence, I think that structure gives us the best chance of making real progress rather than just producing demos.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts embodied intelligence with software and platform work, but does not identify a mismatch between researchers’ view of advanced technology and the technology industry’s needs.

r002.rationale: It favors a focused, startup-like subsidiary with industry partnerships and real-world deployment, but does not clearly endorse pursuing embodied intelligence as a real business over a research-oriented experimental team.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that embodied intelligence has a fundamentally different rhythm from the rest of what we were doing, and if you try to run it inside a larger organization, it gets quietly crushed by that organization's rhythm.

Let me explain what I mean. In the software side of AI, whether that's a foundation model or a product built on top of one, the iteration loop is fast. You train, you evaluate, you ship, you get feedback in days or weeks. Everyone around you is optimized for that cadence: the budgeting, the hiring, the way people are reviewed. Embodied intelligence doesn't work that way. You're dealing with hardware lead times, with data that you can't just scrape from the internet, with the physical world being slow and expensive and unforgiving. A robot falling over costs you real money and real time. If you sit that team next to a team shipping model updates every two weeks, the embodied team always looks like it's underperforming, and eventually it starts getting starved of resources, not because anyone made a bad decision, but because the comparison is unfair.

So the first reason is protection. A subsidiary gives the team its own clock. Its own metrics, its own capital plan, its own definition of what a good quarter looks like.

The second reason is talent. The people who are genuinely excellent at embodied AI are a strange mix. You need roboticists, control people, people who understand mechanical design, simulation people, and then the learning people on top of that. Many of the best ones don't want to be a sub-team inside a company whose center of gravity is somewhere else. They want to feel like the mission is the mission. A separate entity, with its own name and its own identity, makes that recruiting conversation completely different.

The third reason is a bit more strategic. Embodied intelligence is going to need partners that a pure AI company doesn't naturally have: manufacturers, supply chain, maybe eventually customers in logistics or manufacturing. Those partnerships are easier when there's a focused entity across the table, rather than a division whose priorities might shift with the parent's next strategy meeting. It also keeps the option open for the subsidiary to raise capital on its own terms, because the risk profile really is different, and investors who understand hardware are not necessarily the same investors who understand models.

And I'd add one more thing, which is about us internally. It forced clarity. When you spin something out, you have to write down what it is, what it isn't, what success means in three years. That exercise alone was worth a lot. Inside a big org, you can keep an ambiguous project alive for a long time without ever answering those questions.

Now, I don't want to pretend it was risk-free. The obvious danger is that you cut the subsidiary off from the thing that made it worth doing in the first place, which is access to the frontier models and the research culture. We spent a lot of time on that boundary, making sure the data and the model work could still flow both ways. If you get that wrong, you've just created a small, underfunded robotics startup, and the world has plenty of those already.

But on balance, yes, I think it was the right call, mostly because the alternative was slowly suffocating something that needed to breathe at its own pace.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts the fast cadence of software AI with the slower hardware and physical-world demands of embodied intelligence, but does not identify a mismatch between researchers’ view of advanced technology and industry needs.

r002.rationale: It supports creating a focused subsidiary for embodied intelligence, but does not frame that choice as pursuing a real business rather than a research-oriented experimental team.

astra-6.text:
I think the value is focus. Embodied intelligence requires hardware, software, and interaction with the physical world to develop together. That means the team needs a clear mandate and room to experiment, learn from failures, and iterate.

A dedicated subsidiary gives that work its own priorities and accountability, while still allowing it to draw on the parent company’s resources. But the structure alone doesn’t make the decision wise. The real test is whether it helps the team turn research into reliable products that solve practical problems.

You’re bringing together models, hardware, and interaction with the physical world, so those pieces need to be developed closely together. A subsidiary gives the team clear responsibility and room to experiment, while still allowing it to draw on the parent company’s resources. Of course, the structure itself doesn’t guarantee success. The real test is whether it helps the team learn faster and turn the technology into something useful.
